units.text: Let's decide where edge code belongs by following one request. Viewer-request code can act before lookup. That matters if a redirect or normalization must take effect whether or not the object is already cached.

On a miss, CloudFront can call the origin. The origin-request hook acts before that fetch, and origin-response code acts when the response comes back. A hit skips those origin hooks and can still have a viewer response phase.

A lightweight viewer-request function can redirect, rewrite a URI, or normalize a header before lookup. For example, make equivalent paths share one consistent spelling instead of caching unnecessary duplicates.

A viewer-response function can adjust permitted headers as CloudFront prepares a response for the client. Choose the request phase if you need to affect lookup; choosing the response phase would be too late. Supported network helpers can call eligible origins configured on the same distribution.
Use a viewer event for logic close to the user, or an origin event for work that belongs on the origin fetch path. Follow which requests actually pass the event before choosing where to run code.

Associate a published numbered function version in US East, Northern Virginia. CloudFront replicates the version for edge use. Deploy a new version and update the association rather than relying on edits to the unpublished function.

Let's divide work between the two tools without creating an invalid association. For one cache behavior, choose one function family for both viewer-event types. You can pair a CloudFront Function at the viewer with Lambda at Edge for an origin-request or origin-response event.
For example, normalize the viewer request before lookup and reserve origin-request logic for cache misses. Testing only a miss can make an incomplete design look correct; test a hit too.

First ask which trigger and inputs you need. Lambda at Edge supports origin request and response triggers and can inspect a bounded request body when enabled. Those are strong reasons to choose it even when a viewer function handles lightweight logic.

Network access alone isn't a deciding test anymore. On an eligible plan, a CloudFront Function can make one supported fetch or beacon call per invocation to an eligible origin configured on that distribution. If the call or processing you need doesn't fit that environment, compare Lambda at Edge and the origin application instead.

CloudFront Functions is a lightweight JavaScript runtime for viewer events. Lambda at Edge offers more runtime room, other supported languages, and origin hooks. Compare the actual event-specific limits before placing heavier code.

CloudFront Functions can't read the viewer's request body. Lambda at Edge can expose a bounded body when configured. Network support is a separate check: CloudFront Functions now supports constrained calls to distribution-configured origins, not unrestricted network access.
